results.title: Measuring Systemic Banking Resilience: A Simple Reverse Stress Testing Approach
results.journal_or_venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper Series (Policy Research Working Paper 9864); Finance, Competitiveness and Innovation Global Practice
results.abstract_summary: The paper develops a simple, transparent country-level banking resilience metric — the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP) — based on bank-level reverse stress tests that estimate how much non-performing loans would need to rise to deplete capital buffers of the most fragile banks. It applies this approach to public balance-sheet data for over 1,500 banks in 59 emerging market and developing economies during the COVID-19 pandemic and evaluates how the CDBP relates to common macro-financial and financial soundness indicators to show its potential as a complementary surveillance tool.
key_findings: [supported] The paper introduces the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP), a simple country-level reverse stress test metric that quantifies the percentage-point increase in non-performing loans (NPLs) needed to deplete capital buffers for the subset of banks that together represent at least 20% of total banking system assets.
[supported] The authors compute the CDBP for ~1,500 commercial banks across 59 emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) using mostly Q3-2020 (or latest ≤2019) Fitch balance-sheet data.

[supported] The cross-country median CDBP is 9.8 percentage points; in 10 countries a 5 percentage-point increase in NPLs would deplete capital buffers of the 'Banks at Risk'; two countries have 'Banks at Risk' already undercapitalized.

[supported] Regional variation is substantial: South Asia (SAR) shows the lowest median CDBP (3.8 pp) while Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) shows among the highest (14.0 pp unweighted median), with East Asia & Pacific showing a tighter distribution.

[supported] CDBP correlates only weakly with existing country-level banking risk indicators (e.g., Economist Intelligence Unit banking risk index) and with standard financial soundness indicators (FSIs); regressions explain only a modest share of CDBP variation (R-squared up to ~0.31).

[supported] Empirical associations found: higher liquid assets to short-term liabilities is positively associated with CDBP, interest margin is negatively associated, and the NPL ratio is negatively associated when conditioning on multiple FSIs (specific regression coefficients reported).
[supported] Including bank profits as an initial buffer (robustness test) produces very similar CDBP values: the pairwise correlation between the standard and profits-adjusted CDBP is 0.953.

[speculative] The authors recommend using CDBP as a complementary, transparent first-step monitoring tool (particularly where supervisory data are limited or opaque) and as a flag to trigger more in-depth supervisory review.

[speculative] The methodology relies on multiple simplifying assumptions (e.g., a uniform assumed NPL provisioning rate of 55%, no collateral, and in the baseline no profits), which can be relaxed but imply the CDBP is a rough approximation and not a full stress test.

[speculative] The CDBP does not capture contagion, knock-on effects, sovereign-bank feedback loops, or other non-credit shocks and does not provide an estimate of the likelihood or timing of the NPL increases it computes.
results.results_summary: The paper develops and applies a transparent reverse stress-testing metric (CDBP) that identifies how much the consolidated NPL ratio for the most fragile banks (covering at least 20% of system assets) must rise to exhaust capital buffers. Using Fitch bank-level data for ~1,500 banks in 59 EMDEs (mostly Q3-2020), the authors find a cross-country median CDBP of 9.8 percentage points, substantial regional heterogeneity, and only modest correlations with existing financial soundness indicators and banking-risk indices. Robustness checks (including profits as a buffer) produce highly correlated results. The authors conclude the CDBP can complement existing indicators as a simple monitoring tool but emphasize important methodological limitations and advise it be used alongside deeper supervisory analysis.
performance_claims: Sample: approximately 1,500 commercial banks in 59 EMDEs (Fitch data, up to Q3-2020 or latest ≤2019)
Median CDBP across countries: 9.8 percentage points
In 10 countries, a 5 percentage-point increase in NPLs would deplete capital buffers for banks representing ≥20% of assets
Two countries in the sample have 'Banks at Risk' already undercapitalized
Regional medians (unweighted): SSA CDBP = 14.0 pp; EAP CDBP = 13.6 pp; LAC CDBP = 10.5 pp; SAR CDBP = 3.8 pp
Pairwise correlation between baseline CDBP and profits-adjusted CDBP = 0.953
Cross-sectional regressions: R-squared ranges reported up to 0.311 when conditioning on multiple FSIs

Selected regression coefficient (conditional specification): Non-performing Loans to Gross Loans coefficient = -0.577 (statistically significant in reported model), Liquid Assets to Short-Term Liabilities coefficient ≈ 0.213 (statistically significant at conventional levels in reported model)
results.quantum_advantage_detail: This technical report addresses banking-sector reverse stress testing and systemic resilience; it contains no claims about quantum computing or quantum advantage.
limitations: Scope restricted to credit risk only; does not account for liquidity, foreign-exchange, market risk, sovereign-bank nexus, commodity-price shocks, or other non-credit channels (author-stated)
Does not capture interbank interdependencies, knock-on effects, contagion, or non-linear distress propagation across banks (author-stated)
The approach computes an NPL 'breaking point' but does not attach any probability or time horizon to the shock (author-stated)
NPL data are backward-looking, lagged, and may be underreported—especially in jurisdictions with weak supervisory practices (author-stated)
Sample coverage may be incomplete (missing unlisted banks, mutual/state-owned banks, smaller/rural credit institutions and other credit institutions) (author-stated)

Assumes provisions for new NPLs fully absorb capital buffers and that banks have no profits to offset provisioning (conservative assumption; author-stated), although a robustness test including profits is reported

Assumes a uniform NPL provisioning rate of 55% (based on a simple equal-weighting across loan categories) and applies provisions to full NPL exposure ignoring collateral and supervisory haircuts (author-stated)
Does not consider tax implications or potential tax credits that could mitigate capital depletion (author-stated)

Minimum regulatory capital requirement (MCR) data used refer to year-end 2016 and are applied uniformly across banks, ignoring time-varying or bank-specific buffers and other regulatory requirements (author-stated)
The method simplifies the change in risk-weighted assets (RWA) when loans turn NPL and uses aggregate risk-weight density assumptions (author-stated)

Country-level consolidated metric depends on the chosen 20% asset threshold for 'Banks at Risk' (authors note the threshold can be adjusted), which may not be appropriate for all banking systems (author-stated and [inferred])

Empirical application uses Fitch balance-sheet data up to Q3 2020 (or latest available not older than 2019 for some banks), which limits currency and may not reflect post-2020 developments (author-stated and technical-report currency concern)
CDBP associations with standard financial soundness indicators are modest; explanatory power is low, limiting immediate operational interpretability (author-stated)
[inferred] No formal backtesting or out-of-sample predictive validation against historical banking crises or later realized stress outcomes is presented

[inferred] Potential sensitivity of results to key modelling choices (provisioning rate, treatment of collateral, RWA assumptions, choice of buffer definitions, profit treatment) is not fully quantified across a wide range of alternative calibrations
[inferred] Use as a 'simple' indicator may give a false sense of precision given data quality issues and simplifying assumptions

[inferred] As a World Bank Policy Research Working Paper / technical report, it may not have undergone peer review; potential institutional perspective or mandate could influence framing (technical-report-specific)
open_questions: How reliably does the CDBP predict actual banking stress or systemic crises ex post (predictive validity and backtesting)?
How sensitive are CDBP results to alternative provisioning assumptions (e.g., different mixes of substandard/doubtful/loss loans), inclusion of collateral, and alternative RWA treatments?
What is the appropriate asset-share threshold (20% used here) for defining 'Banks at Risk' in different country contexts, and how does varying that threshold affect conclusions?
How can likelihoods and time horizons for the computed NPL increases be attached to make the metric actionable for policy (i.e., convert break points into scenario probabilities)?
How would the inclusion of profits, tax credits, bank-specific capital buffers (e.g., conservation buffers, systemic buffers), and leverage ratio constraints change CDBP assessments?
How can interbank linkages, contagion channels, and non-linear dependencies be incorporated into a similarly transparent metric without losing tractability?
To what extent do data gaps (missing unlisted and small banks, delayed or opaque reporting) bias the CDBP, and what minimum data coverage is required for reliable country-level assessments?
How should the metric be adapted for countries with widespread regulatory forbearance or temporary relief measures that obscure true asset quality?
How frequently must underlying data be updated for the CDBP to remain useful for monitoring in rapidly evolving crises?
How can the CDBP be integrated with other supervisory stress-testing frameworks and early-warning systems to improve overall monitoring and policy response?
future_work: Develop and test extensions of the CDBP that incorporate other risk channels (liquidity, FX, market risk) and the sovereign-bank nexus
Incorporate network models or contagion modules to capture interbank linkages and knock-on effects on the consolidated metric
Perform systematic sensitivity analyses and robustness checks over provisioning rates, collateral assumptions, RWA treatments, inclusion/exclusion of profits, and alternative MCR specifications
Backtest and validate CDBP against historical crisis episodes and out-of-sample stress events to assess predictive power and calibration
Improve data coverage and timeliness: include unlisted and smaller banks where possible, and explore alternative data sources to reduce reporting lags and underreporting
Adapt the metric to account for bank-specific regulatory buffers, leverage requirements, tax effects, and country-specific supervisory practices
Explore probabilistic or scenario-based augmentations that attach likelihoods/time horizons to the computed break points
Assess optimal threshold selection (e.g., alternatives to the 20% asset-share rule) and develop guidance for threshold choice tailored to banking system structure
Integrate CDBP outputs into supervisory workflows (flagging for on-site inspections, asset quality reviews) and evaluate operational uses in real-world monitoring
Update and extend empirical applications beyond Q3 2020 (and the 2019 fallbacks) to cover later pandemic-related dynamics and post-pandemic developments
key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Introduces the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP), a simple, transparent reverse stress-test metric computable from public bank balance-sheet data to quantify the percentage-point increase in NPLs required to exhaust capital buffers for the most fragile banks.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Empirical application to ~1,500 banks across 59 EMDEs yields concrete quantitative summaries (median CDBP = 9.8 pp; regional medians; pairwise correlation 0.953 with profits-adjusted CDBP), demonstrating practical applicability with available data.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Authors position CDBP as a complementary, first-step monitoring tool to flag vulnerabilities and trigger more in-depth supervisory analysis rather than as a standalone stress-test.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Robustness checks (e.g., including profits) and cross-sectional regressions indicate the metric is informative but explains only a modest share of cross-country variation (R-squared up to ~0.31), supporting use alongside other indicators.
